summary:
Visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

What such a passport can contain is constrained. Legal gender change still requires a letter from a medical expert, and the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure that takes between three and nine months. The self-identification bill was withdrawn in July 2025. Since a law passed in December 2013 took effect in 2014, changing gender on birth certificates and other official documents has no longer required surgery or sterilisation, which had been mandatory under the 1984 and 1985 laws.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations is expressly prohibited by the Equal Treatment Act as amended by initiative Law 34.650, adopted by the Tweede Kamer on 3 July 2018 and the Eerste Kamer on 12 March 2019 (64 votes to 11), published 25 September 2019 and in force from 31 October 2019. Before that amendment the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Sexual orientation and disability were formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution in February 2023; gender identity is not among the grounds named there.

Since 1 July 2025 a private-member's bill has placed discriminatory motive into law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, alongside expanded victims' rights. Dutch legislation nonetheless contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through a police Centre of Expertise Discrimination. One comparative database states that hate-crime protections in Dutch law cover sexual orientation only.

Official victimisation figures are substantial. More than 10% of LGBTIQ+ people in the Netherlands have experienced physical or sexual violence, rising to 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism recorded a sharp rise in verbal abuse, intimidation and violence; in 2022 one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.

Police recorded about 4,800 discrimination and violence reports concerning LGBTQIA+ people last year, 7.5% more than in 2024 and 81% above the 2,654 recorded in 2022. Reports concerning transgender people rose 51% in a single year, from 264 to 399. Only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were secured in that year. These are raw counts with no per-capita denominator in the source, so the increase is a trend in reporting rather than a measured rate of risk.

Amsterdam is one data point within that national pattern. Mayor Halsema told the city council that discrimination and violent incidents would be tackled with priority during World Pride 2026, with police, enforcers and organisers agreeing to act fast; recent Prides drew between 25 and 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene. More than 70 people reported discrimination during the opening of WorldPride Amsterdam through the RITA platform, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants, and RITA warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened its 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected.

Detention carries a documented and unresolved exposure. No law, regulation or official policy governs the placement of transgender detainees; the Penitentiary Principles Act separates only male and female detainees. The Prison Service confirmed that placement rests on the gender designation in municipal population records together with case-by-case factors including gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background and physical or mental health, while a specialist body was drafting unpublished guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently held on an 'Extra Care Facility' wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman held on a regular male wing on arrival before transfer to such a wing; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, where she reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; a Limburg district court sentencing ruling of 17 October 2017 concerning a trans woman facing placement in a men's prison; and an appeals court ruling of 29 June 2020 concerning a trans man in a women's prison, the courts treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights advised the Minister for Legal Protection on 21 February 2024 to create rules aligned with international detention-monitoring standards placing transgender detainees by gender identity, and recorded that no official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the country.
tangentialFactors:
The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026, and one comparative database ranks it 2nd of 121 regions as a good place for LGBT people, with 22% support recorded for LGBT openness in its own measure. Public opinion measured directly is more favourable on rights than on lived attitudes: a 2023 Eurobarometer found 91% of Dutch people agreed that transgender people should have the same rights as anyone else and 84% thought transgender persons should be able to change their civil documents to match their gender identity, while a 2016 Netherlands Institute for Social Research report found 10% of Dutch people view transgender people negatively.

Attitudes among young people are moving in the opposite direction. A Utrecht University and Trimbos HBSC study found positive attitudes toward homosexuality among secondary-school boys falling from 40% to 22% and among girls from 78% to 51% between 2021 and 2025.

The rise in reported incidents is a national figure, and Amsterdam's World Pride period is a single concentrated illustration of it rather than the pattern itself. The source provides no general homicide or violence rate against which the 17% transgender physical or sexual violence victimisation figure can be benchmarked, so the magnitude of trans-specific exposure relative to the background rate remains unmeasured.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been administrative since the December 2013 law took effect in 2014, replacing the surgery and sterilisation requirement in force between 1985 and 2014. The state issued a formal apology in December 2020 and implemented a €5,000 compensation scheme that same month for an estimated 2,000 people sterilised under the prior law, following a February 2020 class-action lawsuit and cabinet announcements in November 2020 and November 2021.

The 'X' marker has no general legislation behind it and remains court-decided. Since 1993 a birth certificate may state that sex cannot be determined; the District Court of Limburg granted that designation on 28 May 2018, Leonne Zeegers received a Dutch passport with an 'X' in October 2018 and Nanoah Struik in July 2019, a district court allowed a gender X birth certificate in July 2021, and a December 2021 ruling dropped the psychologist certification requirement for X in passports. In July 2020 the government announced it was considering abolishing gender markers on official identity documents from 2025.

Transgender people may serve openly in the military, a position in place since homosexuality was declassified as a mental illness in 1973. The 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing the harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate.

A bill banning conversion therapy defined as attempting to change sexual orientation or gender identity passed the Tweede Kamer in September 2025, the Eerste Kamer on 16 June 2026 and was ratified on 8 September 2026; such therapies have been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and organisations offering them are ineligible for subsidies.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples began on 1 January 1998 and same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 April 2001, with same-sex joint and stepchild adoption legalised alongside it. Since 2014 all marriage officiants are prohibited from refusing services to same-sex couples. A trans person in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex therefore enters a recognised marriage or partnership, and no officiant may decline it.

Placement of transgender detainees rests on the gender designation in municipal population records plus case-by-case assessment, with no governing law or published policy, and the Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights has asked the Minister for Legal Protection to write rules placing detainees by gender identity.
